study_type.note: Longitudinal IDE telemetry plus survey and interviews.

research_method.claude: Mixed methods: two-year longitudinal IDE telemetry analysis (Mixed Linear Model Regression), online survey (5-point Likert), 5 post-survey semi-structured interviews
research_method.nlm: Mixed methods: longitudinal IDE telemetry analysis, survey, semi-structured interviews
research_method.value: Mixed methods: two-year longitudinal analysis of IDE telemetry (800 devices, 400 AI users vs 400 non-users, 151,904,543 events; monthly trends via Mixed Linear Model Regression) on five workflow dimensions, plus online survey (5-point Likert; 62 valid responses) and 5 follow-up semi-structured interviews
research_method.note: Mixed Linear Model reported only by Claude (not contradicted).

context.claude: Industry; professional developers using JetBrains IDEs (IntelliJ IDEA, PyCharm, PhpStorm, WebStorm), study with JetBrains; 800 devices, 62 survey respondents, 5 interviewees
context.nlm: Industry; professional developers in the JetBrains ecosystem (IntelliJ IDEA, PyCharm, PhpStorm, WebStorm); 800 developers, 62 survey respondents, 5 interviewees
context.value: industry; professional developers using JetBrains IDEs (IntelliJ IDEA, PyCharm, PhpStorm, WebStorm), study run with JetBrains; 800 developers' telemetry (JetBrains AI Assistant users vs non-users), 62 survey respondents, 5 interviewees

space_applied.note: SPACE only referenced (to justify code output as an activity indicator).

ai_discussed.note: In-IDE AI coding assistants are the object of study (AI users vs non-users).

remote_covid.note: Work mode not specified by either.

data_window.note: Claude: logs from October 2022 to October 2024; NotebookLM: only 'over 2 years'. Full text: devices active in Oct 2022 and Oct 2024; trend analysis on October 2022 to September 2024 (24 months).

cat_productivity.note: Typed characters as productivity proxy (RQ1); perceived productivity and coding time in survey.

cat_quality.note: Debugging instances as code-quality proxy; perceived code quality and readability.

cat_collaboration.note: NotebookLM labels external pastes 'Collaboration/Reuse', but code reuse is not a collaboration metric; AI as 'second pair of eyes' only in interview quotes.

cat_satisfaction.note: Claude lists overall satisfaction with AI coding tools (71% satisfied) as a survey metric; NotebookLM does not mention it. In the paper it is a context question alongside reliance on AI.

cat_activity.note: IDE event counts: deletions, external pastes, IDE window activations (and typed characters).

cat_devex.note: Both tag context switching 'DevEx', but the DevEx framework is not used or cited.

cat_survey.note: 5-point Likert survey of perceived changes in the five dimensions, plus interviews.

evidence.quote: We address this gap with a mixed-method study of AI adoption in IDEs, combining longitudinal two-year fine-grained telemetry from 800 developers with a survey of 62 professionals.
We analyze 151,904,543 fine-grained, anonymized IDE interaction logs collected over two years from 800 software developers, including 400 AI users and 400 AI non-users.
Given the non-normal distribution and heteroscedasticity of our data, we performed Mixed Linear Model Regression [39] for trend analysis.
Telemetry reveals that AI users produce substantially more code but also delete significantly more.
As a proxy for productivity, we counted the number of typed characters in the editor (RQ1)
As a proxy for code quality, we chose the number of debugging instances (RQ2).
As a proxy for code editing, we chose the number of deletions, including delete keystrokes, backspaces, undos, etc. (RQ3).
As a proxy for context switching, we chose the number of IDE window activations (RQ5).
Seven 5-point Likert-scale questions regarding perception of their workflow after they started using AI.
